findings.claim: "the Catholic Church has officially recognised 70 miraculous healings at Lourdes" (repeated in L3 practice_questions[5].marks as "and 70 have been recognised")
findings.truth: The Church has recognised 72 cures at Lourdes as miraculous.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Lourdes water ("The Catholic Church has officially recognized 72 miraculous healings from Lourdes"); unit brief

findings.claim: "Philosopher Alvin Plantinga has argued that God is the only plausible candidate for a necessary, uncaused being." given as a strength of the First Cause argument
findings.truth: Plantinga is known for the free will defence, reformed epistemology and a modal version of the ontological argument. No such claim of his about the First Cause argument can be sourced. The point stands without the attribution.
findings.evidence: attribution unverifiable; sentence rewritten without a named philosopher

findings.claim: "the mark scheme specifically requires you to refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching"
findings.truth: The instruction to refer to a source sits in the question itself, not in a mark-scheme rule. Stating it as a mark-scheme requirement is an examiner claim we cannot make.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section, lines 296-306; house rule on examiner claims

findings.claim: "Without naming a source, your answer is capped below the Mastering band regardless of how detailed the rest of your answer is."
findings.truth: The 6-mark question carries one mark for the source. A student who omits the source loses that one mark; the band for the rest of the answer is not capped.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section, lines 302-306 (theme question parts 1, 1, 4, 6, 12)

findings.claim: "Without a conclusion, your answer stays in the Developing band at most."
findings.truth: A missing justified conclusion blocks the top band only. It does not drop the answer to the second-lowest band.
findings.evidence: 12-mark question needs a justified judgement for the top band; house band ladder

findings.claim: 12-mark model answer: "Many scientists such as Swinburne have developed the fine-tuning version of the argument"
findings.truth: Richard Swinburne is a philosopher of religion (Oxford), not a scientist.
findings.evidence: Swinburne, The Existence of God; standard attribution

findings.claim: "Which philosopher criticised the Design argument by arguing that the analogy between a watch and the universe is weak?" options [David Hume, William Paley, Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne] with correct = 1
findings.truth: The critic is David Hume, index 0. Index 1 is William Paley, who made the analogy. The key marks the true answer wrong.
findings.evidence: Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion; lesson content_html says the same

findings.claim: Fill question "The argument that God permits suffering so humans can develop virtues is called the _____ theodicy" with options [free will, soul-making, Augustinian, Irenaean], correct = 1
findings.truth: "Irenaean theodicy" is the standard second name for the soul-making theodicy, so option 3 is also true and a student picking it is marked wrong. The lesson itself links Hick's soul-making theodicy to Irenaeus. Distractor replaced with "natural law" (Aquinas's ethics, not a theodicy).
findings.evidence: lesson content_html n7; standard naming of Hick's theodicy

findings.claim: model answer quotes the Qur'an as "We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss" (2:155)
findings.truth: The verse reads "...with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits". The quotation marks make the short form a misquotation; the lesson content_html quotes it correctly.
findings.evidence: Qur'an 2:155; the same verse quoted in full in L2 content_html n9

findings.claim: "In the creation of the heavens and earth... there are signs for those who reason" (Qur'an 3:190), repeated in practice_questions[4].marks
findings.truth: Qur'an 3:190 ends "signs for those of understanding" (ulu al-albab). "A people who use reason" is the ending of 2:164, a different verse.
findings.evidence: Qur'an 3:190 (Sahih International / Abdel Haleem: "for those with understanding")

findings.claim: "Hume argued that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence"
findings.truth: That phrase is Carl Sagan's (after Laplace), not Hume's. Hume's argument is that no testimony establishes a miracle unless the testimony being false would be more surprising than the miracle itself.
findings.evidence: Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section X; Sagan, Cosmos (1980)

findings.claim: 4-mark question: "Explain two contrasting views on whether the Design argument proves God exists."
findings.truth: For this theme the spec sets contrasting beliefs on visions, miracles and nature as general revelation only, so a contrast question on the Design argument would not be set. It is still useful practice.

findings.claim: "closer to you than your jugular vein" (Qur'an 50:16)
findings.truth: The verse reads "closer to him than his jugular vein". The sense is unchanged and the short form is common in teaching material.

findings.claim: All three lessons carry a second 4-mark question built round a named student (Priya, Layla, Tariq) who is asked to give reasons for a view.
findings.truth: The 4-mark part of this paper's theme question is a contrasting-beliefs question that must refer to Christianity and to another tradition or to non-religious belief. The scenario form is not used on this paper, and the marks are legal, so this is a shape question, not a wrong-marks question. Options: (a) keep them as extra practice, (b) relabel them as practice-only and not exam-form, (c) rewrite all three into the contrasting-beliefs form.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section lines 302-306; spec 3.2.1.3 lines 1299-1305
findings.ruling: Leave: scenario practice kept / band-ladder relabel queue.

findings.claim: The mark schemes use the band ladder Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging.
findings.truth: The checker brief names the house ladder as Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band. This unit's ladder is not a board descriptor and is not a banned string, so it is safe, but it differs from the house set used elsewhere. Options: (a) leave, (b) fold this unit into the band-ladder relabel queue in the retro programme.
findings.ruling: Leave: scenario practice kept / band-ladder relabel queue.

summary: Two answer keys were wrong: the L1 knowledge check marked Paley as the critic of his own watch analogy, and the L2 theodicy fill listed 'Irenaean' as a distractor when it is another name for the correct answer. The rest are exam-claim overstatements in the tips, two misquoted verses (Qur'an 2:155 and 3:190), a Sagan phrase attributed to Hume, an unsourced Plantinga attribution, and the Lourdes cure count (72, not 70).
